title: Fossils & Evolution
intro: Fossils are the preserved evidence of past life. Learn HOW they form (and why so few do), how they date rocks (index fossils), and how evolution, natural selection and extinction explain the changing fossil record.

sections.title: Fossils, fossil ranges and index fossils
bullets: **Fossils** are any evidence of past life preserved in rock: real body parts (rare), impressions, casts and molds, parts replaced by minerals, or signs of behaviour such as footprints and burrows (Textbook 7.3).

Slide 4 (Fig. 10.3) shows **the principle of fossil succession**: fossils appear in the rock layers in a definite order, because life changes through time. Layers 1 to 10 are stacked oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top.
The **fossil range** is the span from a species' **first appearance** to its **last appearance**. Each fossil species has its own unique range, and ranges can overlap.
Slide 5: **FAD** = **first appearance datum**. **LAD** = **last appearance datum**.
**Index fossils** are diagnostic of one particular geologic time. If you find one, you know roughly how old the layer is.

Best index fossils (Textbook 7.4.4): the organism was **geographically widespread** and its species lived only a **narrow time interval**. Microfossils such as **foraminifera** (Cretaceous and Cenozoic) and **conodonts** (Cambrian to Triassic) are very useful.

Slides 8-11 are photos only: a fossil fish, a small fossil reptile next to a penny for scale, a person hammering rock to collect fossils, and a museum drawer of fossil fish, ammonites and a jaw. The idea: fossils are dug out of rock and stored as evidence.

boxes.text: Why does fossil succession work? Species appear (evolve) and disappear (go extinct) and do not come back. So each slice of Earth history has its own mix of species. Where two ranges overlap, the overlap is an even narrower slice of time. Think of a library: each book was printed in one year, so the books on a shelf tell you roughly the year.
FAD = First Appearance Datum. LAD = Last Appearance Datum. In a rock column the oldest layer is at the bottom, so a species' FAD sits lower than its LAD.

Do not mix up a fossil range with an index fossil. A species that lived a very long time is a poor index fossil. A short-ranging, widespread one is the good one. The textbook says the average species lifespan in the fossil record is about a million years.

sections.title: Life on the geologic timeline
bullets: Slide 6 (Fig. 10.10): **life first appeared ~3.8 Ga** and early life was **single-celled**.
**O2 from bacteria built up in the atmosphere by 2 Ga.**
**Around 700 Ma, multicellular life evolved.**
**~542 Ma: first appearance of hard shells.** Shells make fossils much more likely to survive. Life then diversified fast: the **Cambrian explosion**.
Later on the spiral: age of dinosaurs (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous), then age of mammals (Cenozoic).

Slide 7 is the geologic column: **Hadean** (oldest, back to 4,570 Ma = birth of the Earth), **Archean**, **Proterozoic**, then **Phanerozoic**. Hadean + Archean + Proterozoic together are the **Precambrian**. The Phanerozoic starts at 542 on the slide.
Units on slide 7: Ka = thousand years, Ma = million years, Ga = billion years.

boxes.text: Why do shells matter so much? Soft bodies rot or get eaten. Hard shells survive burial, so after 542 Ma the rocks hold many more fossils. Textbook 8.6.2 adds that scientists debate whether the Cambrian explosion is real fast evolution, better preservation of hard parts, or a more complete rock record.

Two numbers for the start of life: slide 6 says ~3.8 Ga for life; slide 23 says the first chemical evidence is ~3.5 Ga and the oldest bacterial cell fossils ~3.2 Ga. Match the number to the wording of the question. Textbook 8.4.3 gives 3.5 Ga for the first well-preserved fossils (stromatolites).
Order to remember: single cells (3.8 Ga), oxygen (2 Ga), many cells (700 Ma), shells (542 Ma). Slow, slow, slow, then BOOM.

sections.title: Types of fossilization
bullets: Slide 12 lists eight types: **frozen or dried body fossils**; **body fossils in amber or tar**; **preserved or replaced bones, teeth and shells**; **permineralized organisms**; **carbonized impressions of bodies**; **molds and casts**; **trace fossils**; **chemical fossils**.
**Actual preservation** (rare): original material kept. Slide 13 is a frozen baby mammoth; slide 14 is an insect in amber. Textbook: mammoth skin and hair in Arctic deposits, insects in amber.

**Preserved or replaced hard parts**: bones, teeth, shells, usually with the original material replaced by new minerals that keep the shape (slides 15-16 show a skeleton and a rock full of shells next to a penny).
**Permineralization**: after burial, groundwater minerals fill all the spaces, even inside cells. **Petrified wood** (slide 18) is the example.
**Molds and casts**: the body dissolves and leaves a cavity (the **external mold**). If the cavity is later filled with sediment or mineral, you get a **cast**.
**Carbonization**: tissue is squeezed, volatiles escape, and only a thin film of **carbon** remains. Leaves and ferns are typical (slide 17 shows fern leaves).
Slide 20 shows tiny, intricate microscopic fossil shells with a scale bar of 0.01 mm. The slide gives no label, so treat it as an example of microfossils (Textbook 7.4.4).

boxes.text: Why do bones and teeth fossilize best? They are already hard and mineral-rich, so they survive burial. Textbook: stronger materials like bone and teeth are the most likely to be preserved, and soft tissue is very rare because bacteria decay it.
Mold = Missing body (a hole). Cast = Copy (the hole filled in, like jelly poured into a jelly mold).

Slides 15-17 and 20 have no captions. Matching each photo to a type here is my reading of the picture (skeleton = bones, shells = shells, ferns = carbonization). Memorize the definitions, not the photos.

sections.title: Trace and chemical fossils: what organisms DID
bullets: **Trace fossils** are indirect evidence: **footprints, burrows**, droppings (**coprolites**) and stomach stones (**gastroliths**). Slide 19 shows footprints pressed in rock.
**Ichnology** is the study of tracks. Dinosaur tracks can show size, **gait**, speed and behaviour (Textbook 7.3.1).
Coprolites and gastroliths give clues about **diet and habitat**.

Slide 22 asks 'What organisms did that are fossils?' and gives three steps: **observation, analogy, analysis**. A reasonable reading: observe the trace, compare it (analogy) with what living animals do, then analyze what it means. The slide gives no more detail.
Slide 12 also lists **chemical fossils**, chemical signals left by life, called **biomarkers** and **isotopes** on slide 23.

boxes.text: Why are trace fossils valuable? One animal can make thousands of footprints but only one skeleton. Footprints also show how it moved, which bones alone cannot.
A burrow or footprint is a trace fossil, NOT a body fossil, even though an animal made it. A coprolite (fossil dropping) is also a trace fossil.

sections.title: How fossils form and why the record is incomplete
bullets: Slide 21 shows the steps: a dinosaur **collapses and dies**; **flesh rots away, bones remain**; **footprints** are left in the mud; the **water level rises** and **sediment buries** the bones and footprints; a **thick sequence of sediments** piles up over the bones and they gradually **fossilize**; later **erosion exposes** the layer of strata containing the bones and footprints.
Key idea: fossils need **burial**, then **time**, then luck that erosion brings them to the surface.
Textbook 7.3: most life today is **soft-bodied or single-celled** and is not likely to be preserved except in unusual conditions.
The **ocean** is the best place for preservation, yet dissolving and **scavenging** can still destroy remains. On land, burial is even less likely.

So the **fossil record is incomplete**: it records only a small percentage of the life that existed. Slide 39 asks about preservation of a lifeform as a fossil: it is a **rare event** and does not occur for most organisms.

Even so, fossils are used for **stratigraphic correlation** (matching same-age layers in different places, using the principle of faunal succession) and to place a formation on the **geologic time scale**.

boxes.text: Why is burial the key step? Buried bones are protected from scavengers, wind and air. Groundwater and pressure then slowly turn them into rock. A body left on the surface is eaten and scattered.

Slide 39 options: (A) happens every day, (B) is a rare event, (C) does not occur for most organisms, (D) all of the above, (E) is not a result of chance and circumstance. (E) is clearly wrong, since chance and circumstance (for example, quick burial) decide everything. The slide does not print its answer. Textbook 7.3 supports (B) and (C).

sections.title: Earliest life: Archean evidence and stromatolites
bullets: Slide 23 (Fig. 11.3): life first appeared in the **Archean**, known from **biomarkers and isotopes**.
**First chemical evidence of life: ~3.5 Ga.**
**Oldest bacterial cell fossils: ~3.2 Ga** (microscope image, scale 10 micrometres).
**Stromatolites**: layered mats of **cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae), appeared ~3.2 Ga on the slide. Slide 24 shows modern-looking stromatolites as dark domes in shallow water.
Cyanobacteria convert **CO2 and H2O** into hydrocarbon food and release a 'catastrophically deadly waste product': **free oxygen**. This changed Earth's atmosphere forever.
Slide 6 adds that O2 had built up in the atmosphere by 2 Ga.

boxes.text: Why was oxygen 'deadly'? Early life did not use oxygen, so the gas was poison to it. The same waste gas later made breathing animals possible.

Slide says stromatolites ~3.2 Ga; Textbook 8.4.3 says the first well-preserved fossils, stromatolites in Australia, are about 3.5 Ga. Use 3.2 Ga from the slide, and know the textbook value. Also: first chemical evidence (3.5 Ga) is OLDER than the oldest cell fossils (3.2 Ga).

sections.title: Ancient sea animals: ammonoids and the Burgess Shale
bullets: Slide 25 is just a video link on **ammonoids vs nautiloids**. Textbook 7.4.4: **ammonoids** are extinct ancient cousins of the pearly **nautilus**, and were the standard index fossil for Triassic correlation.
Slide 26 is a picture chart of common fossil groups: **trilobite, gastropod, bivalve, brachiopod, bryozoan, crinoid, graptolite, ammonite, coral**.
Slide 27 is an artist's picture of a seafloor full of strange animals. The slide does not label it (it looks like a Cambrian scene).

Slides 28-30: **new Burgess Shale site in Kootenay Park**, from a Nature Communications paper (Feb 11, 2014). Slide 29 is a stratigraphic column (Stephen Formation, Cathedral Formation) and slide 30 a collage of soft-bodied fossils.
Textbook 8.6.2: the **Burgess Shale** (found 1909 by Charles Walcott, western Canada) is a **Lagerstatte**, a site of exceptional preservation including **soft body parts**.
The slide message: **new fossils are found all the time**.

boxes.text: Why is a Lagerstatte special? Normally soft bodies are not preserved at all. In rare spots, mud buried animals so well that we can see worms, claws and eyes. That is how we know what Cambrian animals looked like.
Ammonoids and nautiloids are cousins, not the same thing. Nautiloids still live (pearly nautilus); ammonoids are extinct.
Ammonoid = Ancient and gone. Nautilus = Now still here.

sections.title: Evolution and natural selection
bullets: Slide 31: theory of evolution, **'survival of the fittest'**. Slide 32: **evolution happens every day**, and the question 'Why is life so perfect?'
**Charles Darwin** (1809-1882) said life forms evolve into descendant life forms, and **natural selection** is the mechanism (Textbook 7.3.2).
A **species** is a population with shared characteristics that can reproduce **fertile offspring**.
**Variation** inside a population comes from mixing genes in sexual reproduction and from **mutations**.
Individuals with a helpful trait survive long enough to reproduce and **pass the trait on**. If too many fail, the species goes **extinct**.
If populations become **genetically isolated** (for example on an island), they can become separate species. Evolution is a well-established theory, not just a hypothesis.

Slide 33: tree of life with **Bacteria** and **Archaea** (prokaryotic cells) and **Eukarya** (eukaryotic cells: animals, fungi, plants, ciliates, flagellates, slime molds), all branching from 'proto-life'.
Slide 34: **background vs mass extinction**. Background extinction is the steady, normal loss of species; a mass extinction is a sudden loss of an unusually large number of species (Textbook 8.6.2).

boxes.text: Why does life look 'perfect'? Nobody designed it. Only individuals whose traits fit the environment leave offspring, so over many generations the population fits its surroundings. Misfits do not pass on their traits.
VARIATION + SURVIVAL + INHERITANCE = natural selection. Like a sieve: the environment is the sieve and traits are the sand.

'Survival of the fittest' means best fit for the environment AND able to reproduce, not simply strongest or biggest. The slide gives only the quote; this meaning comes from the textbook description of natural selection.

sections.title: Mass extinctions through time
bullets: Slide 35 plots **number of genera** (y-axis, up to ~4,000) against **geologic time in millions of years** (x-axis, 500 to 0).
Five **mass extinctions** are labelled: **O/T**, **Late D (Devonian)**, **P/Tr (Permian-Triassic)**, **Tr/J (Triassic-Jurassic)** and **K/T (Cretaceous-Tertiary)**.
Each mass extinction shows as a **sharp drop** in the red line. The line then recovers.
Overall the line **climbs**, and the number of genera is **highest today** on the graph.
Textbook 8.6.2: the end-Ordovician extinction is the earliest of five mass extinctions in the fossil record. The end of the Paleozoic (Permian) is the **largest** mass extinction in Earth history.

boxes.text: Why does diversity bounce back after each crash? Survivors find empty living space and evolve into new species to fill it. Extinction and evolution work together.

Slide key: T = Tertiary, K = Cretaceous, J = Jurassic, Tr = Triassic, P = Permian, C = Carboniferous, D = Devonian, S = Silurian, O = Ordovician, and the Cambrian symbol on the axis. 'K/T' means Cretaceous/Tertiary, NOT Triassic. The slide gives no percentages, so do not invent any.

sections.title: DNA as a new tool
bullets: Slide 36: **DNA is a new tool** for studying life's past. It cites a 2013 PLoS ONE paper on the first evidence for a **massive extinction event affecting bees close to the K-T boundary**.

Slide 37: **carpenter bees evolved in the Mid Cretaceous**, at the same time as a **dominant type of flowering plants**. The chart is a **chronogram** (family tree drawn against time) with four bee tribes: Manueliini, Xylocopini, Ceratinini, Allodapini.
Slide 38: computer simulations of an extinction event at 65 Mya versus other scenarios, compared with the real bee tree. The slide does not explain the details.
Slide 40 answer: **DNA carries a partial record of an organism's evolutionary history** (D).

Slide 41 answer: many more species exist now because **life has become capable of exploiting a greater diversity of environments** (A). The slides do not print the answers; these are the only options the sources support.

boxes.text: Why is DNA useful? Related species share DNA and differences build up over time. Comparing DNA lets scientists draw family trees and estimate when branches split, even for animals like bees that leave few fossils.
DNA is a PARTIAL record. Choose 'partial record', not 'no record' or 'complete record'. (Textbook 7.3.1 mentions only fragments of DNA from rare dinosaur soft tissue.)
For 'why more species now': life keeps spreading into new habitats. Not gravity, the Sun or luck.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of fossilization listed on slide 12?
quiz.why: Slide 12 lists eight types. Melting by magma would destroy a body, not fossilize it, and is not on the list.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about fossil ranges and index fossils.
I. A fossil range is the span from a species' first to last appearance.
II. Index fossils are diagnostic of a particular geologic time.
III. Every fossil species has exactly the same range.
quiz.why: Slide 4 gives I and II. III is false because each fossil has a unique range.

quiz.q: Why is a widespread, short-lived species a GOOD index fossil?
options: Finding it tells you a narrow slice of time in many places around the world
It is the largest fossil, so it is easy to see
It lived for hundreds of millions of years
It can only be found in one rock layer on Earth
quiz.why: Widespread means you can match layers in many places; short-lived means the match pins down a narrow time interval.

quiz.q: FAD stands for?
quiz.why: Slide 5 defines FAD as first appearance datum and LAD as last appearance datum.

quiz.q: An insect trapped in amber is best classified as which type of fossilization?
options: a body fossil preserved in amber (actual preservation)
quiz.why: Slide 12 lists body fossils preserved in amber or tar. Textbook 7.3.1 gives insects in amber as an example of actual preservation.

quiz.q: Why can petrified wood show fine cell detail?
options: The wood is carbonized into a thin film
Groundwater minerals fill all spaces, even cells, after burial (permineralization)
It forms a hollow external mold only
Magma melts and replaces the wood
quiz.why: Permineralization fills every pore, so the cellulose structure is preserved in detail.

quiz.q: A clam shell dissolves, leaving a cavity in the rock. Later, minerals fill the cavity. What is the filled shape called?
quiz.why: The empty cavity is the external mold; once it is filled the result is a cast.

quiz.q: A fern fossil that is a thin black carbon film on rock is an example of?
quiz.why: Carbonization leaves only a carbon silhouette after volatiles are driven out.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about trace fossils.
I. Dinosaur tracks can give information about size, gait and speed.
II. Coprolites can give clues about diet.
III. Burrows are body fossils.
quiz.why: I and II are in Textbook 7.3.1. Burrows are trace fossils, so III is false.

quiz.q: Why is the fossil record incomplete?
options: Scientists have already found every fossil
Most organisms are soft-bodied or single-celled and burial and preservation are rare
quiz.why: Textbook 7.3: soft-bodied life is rarely preserved, and even in the ocean dissolving and scavenging limit preservation.

quiz.q: Which describes preservation of a lifeform as a fossil?
options: It happens to nearly every organism
It never depends on chance and circumstance
It is guaranteed if the organism has a brain
It is a rare event that does not happen to most organisms
It occurs only in the Cambrian
quiz.why: Slide 39 asks this; Textbook 7.3 says only a small percentage of life is preserved. The slide's answer is not printed, so this is derived from the textbook.

quiz.q: Which gas did cyanobacteria release that 'changed Earth's atmosphere forever'?
quiz.why: Slide 23: they convert CO2 and H2O into food and release free oxygen as a deadly waste.

quiz.q: Slide 6 says life first appeared ~3.8 Ga and the first hard shells ~542 Ma. About how long between these, in billions of years?
quiz.why: 3.8 Ga minus 0.542 Ga is about 3.26 Ga, so about 3.3 Ga.

quiz.q: Why did the fossil record get much richer after ~542 Ma?
options: Soft bodies began to fossilize better than shells
Hard shells appeared and increased fossil preservation
quiz.why: Slide 6: shells increased fossil preservation and life diversified (the Cambrian explosion). Textbook 8.6.2 notes scientists also debate how much is real evolution versus preservation.

quiz.q: In natural selection, why do helpful traits become more common over generations?
options: Individuals with them survive long enough to reproduce and pass them on
The environment changes their DNA to fit
Every individual changes the same amount in one lifetime
quiz.why: Textbook 7.3.2: advantaged individuals are more likely to reproduce and pass favored traits to later generations.

quiz.q: The textbook gives the average lifespan of a species in the fossil record as about?
quiz.why: Textbook 7.3.2: around a million years.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a mass extinction labelled on slide 35?
quiz.why: Slide 35 labels O/T, Late D, P/Tr, Tr/J and K/T.

quiz.q: What does the overall trend of the slide 35 graph tell you?
options: Number of genera has steadily fallen to zero
Biodiversity was highest in the Cambrian
Mass extinctions cause drops, but the number of genera recovers and is highest today
The number of genera stays the same through time
quiz.why: The red line drops at each labelled extinction, then rebounds, and ends highest at the present.

quiz.q: Which statement about DNA within lifeforms is correct (slide 40)?
options: It has no record of their evolution
It is found in most fossils
It cannot be used to explore most organisms
It carries a complete record of every ancestor
It carries a partial record of their evolutionary history
quiz.why: Slides 36-37 use DNA to study bee evolution. DNA is a partial record. The slide's answer is not printed; this follows from slides 36-37.

quiz.q: Many more species exist now than 3, 2, 1 or 0.5 billion years ago because as life has evolved...
options: it has become capable of exploiting a greater diversity of environments
the Sun has become much brighter
it has become luckier as the universe expanded
it has had time to travel across the planet only
quiz.why: Slide 41. Evolution fills new habitats. The slide's answer is not printed; the other options are not supported by any source.

quiz.q: Slide 37 says carpenter bees evolved...
options: in the Mid Cretaceous, at the same time as a dominant type of flowering plants
at the end of the Permian
quiz.why: Slide 37 states it directly.

quiz.q: Which of these is true of the Burgess Shale?
options: It is a Cambrian site in Australia
It is a site of exceptional preservation including soft body parts
It was discovered in 1990 by Darwin
quiz.why: Textbook 8.6.2: Walcott found it in 1909 in western Canada; it is a Lagerstatte. Slide 28 notes a new site in Kootenay Park.

quiz.q: A new layer contains an index fossil whose known range is only the Cretaceous. What can you conclude?
options: The layer is older than every Paleozoic layer
Nothing, index fossils do not help with age
The layer is probably Cretaceous in age
quiz.why: Index fossils are diagnostic of a particular geologic time (slide 4).

quiz.q: Which step in slide 21 comes FIRST in the fossilization of a dinosaur?
options: The dinosaur dies and flesh rots away, leaving bones
A thick sequence of sediments buries the bones
The water level rises and buries footprints
quiz.why: Death and rotting come first, then burial, then fossilization, then erosion exposes the bed.
